title: The revolutions of 1848: the springtime of peoples and the rise of nationalism
group: BHIS-REV — The age of revolutions and empire
examples: Why were there revolutions across Europe in 1848?

events.ask: Why were there revolutions across Europe in 1848?

explain.say: In February 1848 Parisians built barricades, and King Louis-Philippe fled to England. Within weeks there were risings in Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest and Prague. People called it the springtime of peoples. Look at the timeline. Imagine reading every week that another capital had risen.

explain.say: Why then? See the causes. The 1840s were hungry: potato blight and poor harvests pushed up bread prices, and a crash in 1847 cost jobs. Liberals wanted constitutions and a free press. That same February Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto, though few read it at first. Which cause would make a worker join a barricade?

draw.answer: Hunger met new ideas, and news travelled fast.

explain.say: Now the map. Many risings were about nations. Nationalism is the belief that a people sharing language and culture should have its own state. Hungarians under Lajos Kossuth demanded self-rule from Austria, Czechs met in Prague, Italians fought Austria, and Germans elected a parliament in Frankfurt. What happens when two nations claim the same land?

By 1849 the old order was back. See why. Middle-class liberals feared radical workers after the June Days in Paris. Nations clashed, as when Croats fought the Hungarians. Armies stayed loyal to kings, and a Russian army helped crush Hungary. The historian A. J. P. Taylor said German history reached a turning point and failed to turn. Which reason seems decisive?

Yet much lasted: serfdom ended in Austria, Prussia kept a constitution, and Italy in 1861 and Germany in 1871 were united from above by Cavour and Bismarck. Benedict Anderson called nations imagined communities, built by print and schools. Brilliant work. Challenge: explain why a nation can feel ancient yet be quite modern.

faq.q: Why were there revolutions across Europe in 1848?
faq.a: Bad harvests and potato blight from 1845, an economic crisis in 1847, liberal demands for constitutions and a free press, nationalist demands for self-rule, and fast news by rail and newspaper combined to set off risings in many capitals.

Liberals and workers split, especially after the June Days in Paris; national groups fought each other; armies stayed loyal to monarchs; and Russia sent an army to help Austria defeat Hungary in 1849.

The idea that a people sharing language, culture or history form a nation that should govern itself in its own state. Benedict Anderson called nations imagined communities, and Ernest Gellner linked nationalism to industrial society and mass schooling.
asks: What did Benedict Anderson mean by imagined communities?

faq.a: An elected assembly that met in Frankfurt from May 1848 to draw up a constitution for a united Germany. In 1849 it offered the crown to the King of Prussia, who refused, and the parliament collapsed.
asks: Why did the Frankfurt Parliament fail?

faq.a: The leader of the Hungarian revolution of 1848 to 1849, which sought self-government from Austria. Austrian and Russian armies defeated it in August 1849 and Kossuth went into exile.

facts: King Louis-Philippe of France abdicated in February 1848.
Metternich resigned as Austria's chancellor in March 1848.
The Communist Manifesto was published in February 1848.

quiz.say: Which outside power helped Austria crush the Hungarian revolution in 1849?
quiz.show: Austria defeated Hungary with help from…
quiz.why: Tsar Nicholas I sent a large army that helped defeat Hungary in August 1849.

wrong.1: Britain did not send troops; it gave Kossuth refuge later.
wrong.2: France was busy with its own revolution and new republic.

quiz.say: What does Benedict Anderson mean by calling nations imagined communities?

options.show: Communities people feel part of without meeting most members

quiz.why: Members never meet most fellow citizens, yet print, schools and symbols make them feel one people.

wrong.1: Anderson stresses nations are powerful and real in effect, not fake.
wrong.2: He means newspapers and print helped, not that nations exist only in books.
